newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN CURRENT, CAPITAL ACCOUNTS TURN CORNER. [CORRECTED 15:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN CURRENT, CAPITAL ACCOUNTS TURN CORNER. [CORRECTED 15:50 GMT]

text.p: South Africa's current account and capital account improved sharply in the fourth quarter of last year, underscoring the economy's recovery after the shock of the rand's precipate fall earlier in the year.

The Reserve Bank's latest Quarterly Bulletin showed the deficit on the current account of the balance of payments narrowed sharply to 4.7 billion rand on a seasonally adjusted and annualised basis in the fourth quarter of 1996 from 8.6 billion in the third quarter and 12.9 billion in the second (corrects time period from the third).
As a result, the country ended the year with a current account deficit of 8.5 billion rand, down from 10.2 billion in 1995.
The central bank said the improvement reflected a substantial increase in the volume of exports as well as an increase in the rand value of gold exports.

The time delay of the anticipated J-curve response to the rand's fall -- which presupposes the current account deteriorates first before improving after devaluation -- had proved relatively short, it said.
"A healthy improvement in the current account balance was in progress within approximately six months after the start of the rand depreciation."

Manufacturing exports put in a particularly strong showing and the value of manufactured goods as a percentage of total merchandise exports rose to 29.5 percent in 1996, compared with 26 percent in 1994.
At the same time, inflows of capital into South Africa jumped sharply in the fourth quarter of 1996, largely due to offshore borrowing by commercial banks.

Short-term capital inflows totalled 4.5 billion rand in the three months to December, after outflows of 0.7 billion in the previous quarter. This more than offset long-term capital outflows of 1.2 billion, leading to a net gain of 3.3 billion.

"The principal contributing factor to the abrupt reversal of short-term capital flows in the fourth quarter was the offshore borrowing activity of private banking institutions," the central bank said.

In the third quarter banks cut their short-term liabilities by 0.4 billion rand but then increased them by 8.6 billion in the fourth quarter, prompted by the high domestic money market shortage and the perceived favourable cost of foreign short-term credit facilities.
As a result of the sharp inflow of capital towards the end of the year, South Africa saw a net inflow of 3.9 billion rand in total capital in 1996.

That was well down on the 19.2 billion recorded in 1995 but that fact that a net inflow occurred at all was "quite remarkable in view of the frequent speculative attacks on the rand during 1996", the Reserve Bank said.
